lesson.title: Read, Write, Append, or Create: Choosing a File Mode
lesson.summary: The mode you pass to open() tells Python whether to read an existing file, overwrite one, add onto the end of one, or refuse to touch one that already exists, and getting it wrong is a fast way to lose data by accident.
lesson.body:
When you open a file, you have to tell Python what you intend to do with it, because reading, writing, and creating a file are three very different operations that need different permissions and behave differently around data that is already there. This intention is the mode, the second argument to `open()`, and choosing the wrong one is one of the most common ways a beginner accidentally destroys data they meant to keep.

`"r"` means read. It is the default mode if you leave the second argument off entirely, and it expects the file to already exist. If it does not, `open()` raises a `FileNotFoundError`, as you saw in the previous chapter. `"w"` means write, and it is the mode most likely to surprise someone: if the file already exists, opening it with `"w"` immediately erases everything inside it, truncating it down to nothing, before you have written a single character. If the file does not exist yet, `"w"` creates it. `"a"` means append: like `"w"`, it will create the file if needed, but if the file already has content, `"a"` leaves that content alone and adds anything you write to the very end. `"x"` means exclusive creation: it creates a brand new file, but if a file with that name already exists, it refuses and raises a `FileExistsError` instead of touching it. `"x"` exists specifically for situations where overwriting an existing file by accident would be a serious mistake.

Any of these letters can be combined with `"b"` for binary mode, as in `"rb"`, `"wb"`, `"ab"`, or `"xb"`. Without `"b"`, a file is opened in text mode, and Python handles it as strings of characters, decoding and encoding text automatically. With `"b"`, a file is opened in binary mode, and Python hands you raw bytes instead of strings, which matters for files that are not text at all, like images or audio. Everything in this chapter sequence sticks to plain text mode, since that covers the large majority of what you will do with files early on.

```python
file = open("log.txt", "w")
file.write("first entry\n")
file.close()

file = open("log.txt", "a")
file.write("second entry\n")
file.close()

file = open("log.txt", "r")
print(file.read(), end="")
file.close()

try:
    open("log.txt", "x")
except FileExistsError as error:
    print("Cannot create:", error)
```

```python
first entry
second entry
Cannot create: [Errno 17] File exists: 'log.txt'
```

Walk through this line by line. The first `open("log.txt", "w")` creates `log.txt` and writes `"first entry
"` into it, then closes it. The second `open("log.txt", "a")` does not erase that first entry, it opens the same file in append mode and adds `"second entry
"` after it. Reading the file back with `"r"` shows both lines together, in the order they were written. Finally, trying to open the same file with `"x"` fails immediately, because `log.txt` already exists, and Python raises a `FileExistsError` rather than letting you accidentally overwrite it. That is the safety net `"x"` is built for.
